title: 1 Chronicles 6:16–30
context: 1 Chronicles 6:16–30 lists the families of Levi’s three sons, Gershom, Kohath, and Merari, tracing several generations of each. The spelling Gershom here and Gershon in 6:1 are two forms of the same name. The Kohathite list includes Elkanah and the sons of Samuel, placing Samuel’s family among the Levites, while 1 Samuel 1:1 introduces Samuel’s father Elkanah as a man of the hill country of Ephraim. Names in these lists also differ in places from the parallel genealogies later in the chapter (6:33–47) and from Exodus 6:16–25 and Numbers 3:17–20. These notes name the differences without harmonizing them. Both traditions read the unit as showing that God remembered the families he set apart for service at his sanctuary.

verses.text: The sons of Levi: Gershom, Kohath, and Merari.
verses.arminianNotes: The unit begins again with Levi’s sons, Gershom, Kohath, and Merari. Arminians note that the spelling Gershom here and Gershon in 6:1 are forms of the same name, and the repetition starts a broader list of all the Levitical families.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the chapter moving from the high priestly line to the whole tribe. Both traditions read the repetition as an organizing device rather than a contradiction.

verses.text: These are the names of the sons of Gershom: Libni and Shimei.
verses.arminianNotes: Gershom’s sons are Libni and Shimei, matching Exodus 6:17. Arminian readers see the genealogy giving each branch of Levi its place, so that every family has a part in God’s service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s ordering of the tribe reaching each family. Both traditions treat the verse as straightforward genealogy that underlines the dignity of all Levitical service.

verses.text: The sons of Kohath were Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel.
verses.arminianNotes: Kohath’s sons are Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel, repeating 6:2. Arminians see the repetition as setting the Kohathite families in their place within the full tribal list.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as part of a careful structure. Both traditions note that Kohath’s line includes both the priests and important Levitical families, which the chapter goes on to describe.

verses.text: The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are the families of the Levites according to their fathers’ households.
verses.arminianNotes: Merari’s sons are Mahli and Mushi, and these are the Levite families by their fathers’ households. Arminian readers see the summary closing the first generation of the list and marking the families who will serve.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the phrase about fathers’ households as emphasizing ordered family service. Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about God’s arrangement of his worship.

verses.text: Of Gershom: Libni his son, Jahath his son, Zimmah his son,
verses.arminianNotes: Gershom’s line runs through Libni, Jahath, and Zimmah. Arminians note that the names here differ in places from the Gershonite line given for Asaph in 6:39–43, and they read the lists as complementary records without forcing them to match.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and also decline to harmonize the differences. Both traditions see the verse continuing the record of families God set apart for sanctuary service.

verses.text: Joah his son, Iddo his son, Zerah his son, and Jeatherai his son.
verses.arminianNotes: The Gershonite line continues through Joah, Iddo, Zerah, and Jeatherai. Arminian readers see generations of service preserved by name, honoring families whose work at the sanctuary is otherwise unrecorded.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s faithfulness in remembering these families. Both traditions treat the names as a record of service rather than material for speculation.

verses.text: The sons of Kohath: Amminadab his son, Korah his son, Assir his son,
verses.arminianNotes: Kohath’s line is given through Amminadab, Korah, and Assir. Arminians note that elsewhere Korah is called a son of Izhar (6:37–38; Exodus 6:21), and they name the difference without trying to resolve it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and likewise leave the difference unharmonized. Both traditions note that Korah’s rebellion (Numbers 16) did not end his family’s line, since his descendants later served as singers.

verses.text: Elkanah his son, Ebiasaph his son, Assir his son,
verses.arminianNotes: The line continues through Elkanah, Ebiasaph, and Assir. Arminian readers see the family of Korah continuing to serve after their ancestor’s judgment, a picture of God’s mercy to later generations (compare Numbers 26:11).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s grace preserving the family. Both traditions read the verse as showing that judgment on one man did not cut off his descendants from God’s service.

verses.text: Tahath his son, Uriel his son, Uzziah his son, and Shaul his son.
verses.arminianNotes: The line continues through Tahath, Uriel, Uzziah, and Shaul. Arminians note that these names differ in places from the parallel line in 6:36–37, and they treat the two lists as separate records without forcing agreement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and also leave the differences as they stand. Both traditions read the verse as part of the Kohathite record that leads toward Samuel and Heman.

verses.text: The sons of Elkanah: Amasai and Ahimoth.
verses.arminianNotes: The sons of Elkanah are Amasai and Ahimoth. Arminian readers see the genealogy branching through Elkanah, preparing to trace the family that leads to Samuel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as a transition. Both traditions treat the name Elkanah, which recurs several times in this line, as a family name passed down through the generations.

verses.text: As for Elkanah, the sons of Elkanah: Zophai his son, Nahath his son,
verses.arminianNotes: Elkanah’s line continues through Zophai and Nahath. Arminians note that Zophai is often compared with Zuph in 6:35 and 1 Samuel 1:1, though they avoid treating the comparison as settled.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and hedge any identification. Both traditions read the verse as part of a family record whose details are not always clear, and they avoid harmonizing it with other lists.

verses.text: Eliab his son, Jeroham his son, and Elkanah his son.
verses.arminianNotes: The line continues through Eliab, Jeroham, and Elkanah. Arminian readers recognize Jeroham and Elkanah as names from Samuel’s family in 1 Samuel 1:1, where Elkanah is introduced as a man of the hill country of Ephraim.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that Chronicles here places Samuel’s family among the Levites. Both traditions name the difference from 1 Samuel 1:1 by reference and do not harmonize it.

verses.text: The sons of Samuel: the firstborn, Joel, and the second, Abijah.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel’s sons are Joel, the firstborn, and Abijah, the second. Arminians recall that these sons served as judges but did not walk in their father’s ways (1 Samuel 8:1–3), a reminder that faithfulness is not inherited.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see Samuel’s place in the Levite genealogy honoring his service at the sanctuary. Both traditions note that the names match 1 Samuel 8:2.

verses.text: The sons of Merari: Mahli, Libni his son, Shimei his son, Uzzah his son,
verses.arminianNotes: Merari’s line runs through Mahli, Libni, Shimei, and Uzzah. Arminian readers note that this Uzzah is a Levite in a genealogy, and the text does not identify him with the Uzzah of 2 Samuel 6.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and avoid connecting the two without evidence. Both traditions read the verse as part of the record of Merarite families who carried out sanctuary duties.

verses.text: Shimea his son, Haggiah his son, Asaiah his son.
verses.arminianNotes: The line continues through Shimea, Haggiah, and Asaiah. Arminians see the end of the family list, which has given each branch of Levi its place before the chapter turns to the musicians.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as a transition. Both traditions see the completed family lists as a testimony to God’s ordering of the whole tribe for his service.
